doc.title: Neal Caine interviewed by Monk Rowe, New Hartford, New York, September 26, 2019

title: Advice to young bassists and finding your own sound
summary: Caine advises students to differentiate themselves and be honest; discussion of Buster Williams and the Neal Caine sound.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: So if you were a guest at one of the larger jazz schools, would you have advice? I want to say it was a gathering of bass players at Berklee, right? And you’ve been out in the business for years. Do you have anything you can tell them?

I mean I would say, well you know what I did too, I started bass a little late. Like I was a violin teacher, I mean a violin player. And I remember I was like a teenager. And you know Christian McBride’s maybe my age, maybe a year or so older. But he was kind of like a hot — I just remember looking at him and some other musicians and being like wow, those bass players are great. Like technically, I don’t know if I’m going to be that. So I thought to myself how can I distinguish myself you know. And so I figured oh I’m just going to have the biggest sound out here, I’m going to have the biggest tone and swing the hardest. I would tell those guys to find out what you do good and what you can do to differentiate yourself from the 20,000 other bass players who are playing. I mean besides playing pretty notes and learn changes and be a good bass player. I mean be yourself. It’s like everything has been done basically. Right? So my thing is all we can do is be ourselves, like be true artists, really express yourself, your experience. That’s what it’s about for me.

Yeah, I have often thought that the bass is one of the harder instruments to show a personality. And there’s people that stick out in my mind, like Buster Williams, who God almighty, the sound he had. And I don’t know if it’s just ‘cause partly they knew how to record him or something, but.
No. Well they probably did, but it’s ‘cause he has a unique big ass sound that, you know it’s him instantly. Right?
I’m sorry, did I interrupt you?
No. So what is the Neal Caine sound?

I just — you know what it’s like, I love I appreciate, like we said there’s so many great musicians who know every Paul Chambers solo and John Coltrane solo and can play fast and do this and that. I’m always impressed. But when I hear a musician, whether it be bass or anything, who, they play some, it may be simple, it may even be bad, but I can tell they thought it up, like I can tell it’s from them. It’s organically from them, or that they believe it. That means a lot and I think the audience knows that. And I think a lot of people don’t have that. And I appreciate that. I just like people to be honest. I mean if I want to, you know, like I really respect all these musicians but if I want to go hear — I’ll go listen to Charlie Parker you know or Trane or I mean, we all have influences. I’ll play
a bunch of Israel Crosby shit that’s influenced by him. But I don’t know, I just try to be honest. And I think the audiences feel that.
